query: Which components should be treated as load-bearing when assessing a proposed floor opening, and what must happen before any cutting?
answer_summary: The source identifies the slab, supporting beams, columns, and beam-column connections as load-bearing elements unless an approved design review establishes otherwise. The engineer must assess the opening and specify temporary works before cutting; any required props must be installed and inspected first and retained until release is authorized.

source_document.page_title: Identifying Load-Bearing Elements Before Creating a Floor Opening
source_document.html_content:
Identifying Load-Bearing Elements Before Creating a Floor Opening

Load path review

Before forming an opening in a reinforced-concrete floor, review the approved structural drawings and verify the proposed work area against the structure on site. The floor slab transfers load to supporting beams, and the beams transfer load to columns. Treat beams, columns, and beam-column connections as load-bearing components unless the approved design review establishes otherwise; appearance alone is not a reliable basis for classification.

Risk and temporary support

Cutting a beam or disturbing a beam-column connection without an approved assessment can interrupt the load path and cause local or progressive instability. The project structural engineer must assess the proposed opening and specify any required temporary works before cutting begins.

Where the approved temporary-works design requires props beneath the affected slab, install and inspect them before cutting. Keep the props in place until the opening work is complete, debris and imposed loads have been removed as specified, and the engineer has authorized their release.

query: What order should be followed when removing the wall, and when can its temporary restraint be taken out?
answer_summary: Install and verify the designed restraint before removing masonry where the wall restrains an adjoining element. After service isolation, dismantle from the top downward in small sections. Keep the restraint in place until the structural engineer confirms the retained structure is independently stable.

source_document.page_title: Controlled Removal of a Masonry Wall Adjacent to a Retained Structure
source_document.html_content:
Controlled Removal of a Masonry Wall Adjacent to a Retained Structure

Planning and restraint

Before work begins, confirm from the approved demolition plan that the wall is scheduled for removal and identify any connections to the retained structure. The sequence must be reviewed by the project structural engineer. Where the wall provides restraint to an adjoining element, install the designed temporary restraint and verify it is secure before removing masonry.

Removal sequence

Remove finishes and services attached to the wall only after they have been isolated or disconnected. Dismantle the masonry from the top downward in small, controlled sections; do not create an unsupported panel by removing the lower portion first. Keep the temporary restraint in place while the adjoining element depends on it. Remove the restraint only after the structural engineer confirms that the retained structure is independently stable.

Stability risk

Removing a wall that restrains an adjoining return or floor edge before installing the specified restraint can cause out-of-plane movement or local collapse. This is a high-severity condition where the adjoining element has no other verified lateral restraint.

query: What stability measures and dependencies apply while roof trusses are being removed?
answer_summary: Roof trusses are a connected system whose stability may depend on longitudinal bracing and adjacent connections. Install and verify the engineered temporary bracing before disturbing restraint, follow the planned bay and truss sequence, retain designated bracing and adjacent trusses through each stage, and remove temporary bracing only after the engineer confirms stability.

source_document.page_title: Maintaining Roof Stability During Truss Removal
source_document.html_content:
Maintaining Roof Stability During Truss Removal

Structural arrangement

Roof trusses act as a connected system. Their stability may depend on longitudinal bracing and on connections to adjacent trusses and supporting walls. The demolition plan must identify the trusses and bracing to be retained at each stage; do not assume a truss is stable as an isolated unit.

Temporary stability and sequence

Before removing any roof covering or truss component that contributes to restraint, install the temporary bracing specified in the engineered demolition plan and verify its connections. Remove roof covering in the planned bays while maintaining the required bracing. Dismantle trusses individually in the sequence shown in the plan, retaining the designated bracing and adjacent trusses until the relevant stage is complete. Remove temporary bracing only after the engineer confirms that the remaining roof system is stable.

Hazard

Removing a bracing member or adjacent truss ahead of the planned sequence can destabilize the remaining roof system and lead to lateral movement or collapse. The demolition supervisor must stop work if actual connections or bracing differ from the plan and obtain an engineering review before proceeding.
